excerpt: Reading a charger label, spotting a cable that is about to fail, and the socket habits that stop a small spark becoming a fire.

body.text: This lesson is about chargers, cables, and the small blue spark at the socket. You will read a charger label, recognise a cable that is about to fail, and stop a spark from becoming something worse.
A charger converts the wall's power into the voltage a device needs. When the label does not match the device, or the cable is damaged, the device pays for it.
Before you start

items: Two or three chargers from around the house.
The device each one belongs to.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Reading the label

items: Find the small print on the charger, which lists input and output.
The output shows volts and amps, such as 5V 2A.
Match the volts exactly, since too many volts damages the device.
The amps may be equal or higher, since the device takes what it needs.
A laptop charger shows a wattage, such as 65W, which must match or exceed the original.
The plug shape matters less than the figures printed beside it.

body.text: You will see the output line printed in the smallest text on the charger, often on the side away from the plug. Photograph it, so you can compare it in a shop without carrying the charger.

body.alt: A charger label showing input and output voltage and current.
body.caption: The output line is the one that matters. Volts must match, and amps may be higher.

body.text: It looks like any charger with the right plug will do. The plug fits many devices, and the voltage inside is what the device cares about.
Cables that are about to fail

items: A bend near the plug where the outer cover has split.
A charger that only works when the cable is held at an angle.
Warmth along the cable after a few minutes of charging.
A connector that wobbles, or pulls out with no resistance.
A cable that has been taped, which hides damage rather than repairing it.
A plug with bent pins or a cracked casing.

body.text: The cable will often show a kink close to the connector, which is where the inner wires break first. Replace it rather than bending it into position each time.
A small red mark appears on the switch when the socket is on, and that mark is the check before you plug anything in. Turning it off first removes the spark that most people see at the wall.

body.alt: A three-pin plug with the earth pin visible and the wiring cover removed.
body.caption: Three pins, one of them earth. A plug with a missing earth pin is a shock waiting for a damp day.

body.text: The spark at the socket
A small spark when you plug something in is common, and a large one, or a smell, is not.

items: Switch the socket off before inserting or removing a plug.
Hold the plug by the body, never by the cable.
Avoid daisy-chaining one extension into another.
Keep the total load within what the extension is rated for.
Replace a socket that is loose, discoloured, or warm to the touch.
Call an electrician for a burning smell, which is never a wait-and-see.

body.text: None of this needs an electrician for the ordinary case. Switching off before plugging in removes most of the sparks people see.
Do not worry about replacing a cable that still works. A slightly slow charge is not a danger, and a warm, split, or wobbling cable is.

body.alt: A multimeter measuring the output of a laptop charger at the barrel jack.
body.caption: A multimeter confirms the output when a charger behaves oddly. A repair shop will do this in a minute.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a safety decision, and the first step is always to unplug.

items: The charger is hot enough to hurt: stop using it, and replace it.
The socket sparks every time: switch off at the main, and call an electrician.
The plug is discoloured: that is heat damage. Replace both the plug and the socket.
The laptop charges only at an angle: the cable or the port is failing, so try another cable first.
The charger buzzes: the internal parts are failing, and a replacement costs less than a repair.
A child can reach the socket: fit a cover, which costs almost nothing.

body.text: Practice
Read three labels and check three cables.

items: Photograph the output label of each charger.
Match each one to its device.
Run a finger along each cable, feeling for splits.
Replace the worst cable this week.
Switch the socket off before the next plug you insert.

body.text: You can now charge safely, in a house with an unstable supply. In the next lesson you will meet the blue screen and the spinning circle.

excerpt: What a blue screen is telling you, the stop code worth photographing, and how safe mode gets a machine working again.

body.text: This lesson is about the blue screen and the spinning circle. You will learn what each one means, which detail to photograph, and how safe mode gets a machine started when nothing else will.
A blue screen is Windows stopping on purpose, because continuing would risk the files. It is a protective stop rather than a crash for its own sake.
Before you start

items: The laptop, and a phone for photographs.
The last thing you installed or changed.
About thirty minutes.

body.text: Photograph the screen

items: Take a photograph of the whole screen with the phone.
Note the stop code, a short word in capitals, such as CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED.
Note the date and time, and what you were doing.
Note whether it happens at startup or after a few minutes of work.
Write down the last program you installed.
Keep the photograph, since the screen disappears when the machine restarts.

body.text: You will see the stop code in the lower half of the blue screen, often with a QR square beside it. That code is the only part a repair shop needs, and it is gone in thirty seconds.

The startup screen will show a manufacturer logo and then the circle, and the drive light beside the power button tells you whether work is still happening. A light that flickers is a machine still trying, and a light that stays dark is a machine that has stopped.

body.alt: A phone photographing a blue screen with a stop code.
body.caption: The photograph is the whole investigation. A stop code written down beats a description of the colour.

body.text: It looks like the blue screen means the machine is finished. Most blue screens come from a driver, a memory fault, or a failing update, and all three are repairable.
The spinning circle
A circle that spins for a minute is normal. A circle that spins for ten is a startup that has stalled.

items: Wait five minutes before touching anything, since a slow disk does catch up.
Watch for the hard drive light, which shows whether work is still happening.
Disconnect external devices, since a faulty memory stick stalls startup.
Hold the power button for ten seconds, then start again.
If it happens twice, start in safe mode rather than repeating the loop.
Note what changed before the first time it happened.

body.text: None of this needs a technician. Waiting, unplugging, and a forced restart solve most stalled startups, and each step costs a minute.
Do not worry about losing files by forcing a restart. Windows saves work as it goes, and the risk of a forced restart is far lower than the risk of leaving a stalled machine on all night.

body.alt: A Windows advanced startup menu with the safe mode option highlighted.
body.caption: Safe mode starts with a basic driver set. If the machine works there, the problem is a driver or a new program.

body.text: Safe mode

items: Hold Shift while choosing Restart from the power menu.
Or interrupt the startup three times, which brings the recovery menu.
Choose Troubleshoot, then Advanced options, then Startup settings.
Choose Safe mode, and let the machine start.
Uninstall the program or driver you added most recently.
Restart normally and see whether the fault returns.

body.text: The safe mode desktop will look plain, with large icons and no wallpaper, and some programs will not open. That plainness is the point: it proves the hardware works.

body.alt: Device Manager with a driver's properties open at the rollback button.
body.caption: A driver rollback undoes one update. It is the fastest fix when the fault began the day a driver changed.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and the photograph makes each one easier.

items: It blue screens repeatedly: note the code, and search for that exact code.
It will not start at all: use the recovery menu and choose a restore point.
Safe mode works but normal mode does not: uninstall the newest driver, then restart.
The memory is suspect: a repair shop can test it in an hour.
It happens only in one program: that program or its driver is the cause.
Nothing works: back up the drive from another machine before reinstalling Windows.

body.text: Practice
Learn the recovery route before you need it.

items: Find the Shift and Restart combination in the power menu.
Note what the advanced options screen offers.
Check whether a restore point exists.
Write down the last program you installed.
Practise photographing a screen with the phone.

body.text: You can now meet a blue screen without panic. In the next lesson you will work out whether more memory would help.

excerpt: Whether more memory will help your machine: reading the usage figure, matching the type, and the point where an upgrade is wasted money.

body.text: This lesson helps you decide whether more memory will help your laptop. You will read the usage figure, match the correct type, and recognise the point where an upgrade is wasted money.
Memory holds what the machine is working on right now. When it is full, the machine swaps to the disk, which is far slower, and everything crawls.
Before you start

items: The laptop, with the programs you normally use open.
A note of the current memory size.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Read the numbers

items: Open Task Manager, then Performance, then Memory.
Read the total installed, such as 4.0 GB or 8.0 GB.
Read the in-use percentage while your normal programs run.
Look for the committed figure, which shows what the system needs.
Check whether the disk is at a hundred per cent, which is the real cause of slowness.
Note the number of slots used, which decides whether you add or replace.

body.text: You will see memory sitting above eighty per cent with your usual programs open, which is the sign that more would help. A figure near forty per cent means memory is not your problem.

The performance screen will show the memory graph as a line, and the line climbing to the top while you work explains the pauses. A graph that stays in the lower half means the money is better spent on a drive.

body.alt: Task Manager showing memory usage and slots used.
body.caption: In use, committed, and slots used. The slots figure tells you whether you can add a stick or must replace one.

body.text: It looks like more memory makes any machine faster. A slow machine with free memory needs a new drive, not more memory, and that mistake costs money.
The honest arithmetic

items: Four gigabytes is tight for a modern browser with several tabs.
Eight gigabytes suits ordinary office work and study.
Sixteen gigabytes suits design, video, and many browser tabs.
Going from four to eight is a large, visible improvement.
Going from eight to sixteen helps only if the usage figure is already full.
Going beyond sixteen on an old laptop is usually wasted money.

body.text: None of this needs a new laptop. A memory stick and a solid-state drive, fitted in an hour, restore most five-year-old machines to useful work.
Do not worry about opening the machine. The panel is held by two screws on most models, and a shop will fit the stick for a small fee if you prefer.

body.alt: Two memory sticks showing different notch positions.
body.caption: The notch position differs between generations. A stick that will not seat is usually the wrong type, not a faulty one.

body.text: Matching the type
Memory must match the machine's generation, speed, and physical size. Buying the wrong type is the most common mistake.

items: Check the laptop's specification on the maker's page, using the model number.
Note whether it takes DDR3, DDR4, or DDR5, which are not interchangeable.
Note the size: most laptops use the shorter SODIMM sticks.
Note the speed, such as 2400 or 3200, since mixing speeds can fail.
Buy a matched pair if you are replacing both slots.
Keep the receipt, in case the machine does not accept the stick.

body.alt: A memory stick being seated into a laptop at an angle before pressing down.
body.caption: Seat it at an angle, then press until the clips click. Forcing it flat bends the contacts.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a known outcome, and each has a plain answer.

items: The machine will not start after fitting: reseat the stick, and check the clips clicked.
It starts but shows the old amount: the stick is not seated, or the slot is disabled.
It beeps and stops: the type is wrong, so check the notch and the generation.
It works but crashes: mixed speeds, or a faulty stick. Remove the new one and test.
The machine is under warranty: ask the maker before opening it.
You bought the wrong size: return it unopened, since most shops allow that.

body.text: Practice
Read your own numbers before buying anything.

items: Open Task Manager and note the total memory.
Open your usual programs and read the percentage.
Note the slots used and the speed.
Look up the model number on the maker's site.
Decide whether memory or the drive is the better spend.

body.text: You can now spend on the machine where it helps. In the next lesson you will meet the engineer who fixes these things for a living.

excerpt: Taking a machine for repair: what to photograph before it leaves, what to ask at the counter, and the part you should ask them to return.

body.text: This lesson prepares you to leave a device with a repair engineer. You will photograph what matters, ask three questions at the counter, and keep the paperwork that settles a dispute.
Most repair disputes are about what the machine was like when it arrived, and what was replaced. Both are settled by a photograph and a written receipt, and both take five minutes.
Before you start

items: The device, and the fault described in one sentence.
A phone for photographs.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Photograph it before it leaves

items: Photograph the whole device, front and back.
Photograph the serial number and the model sticker.
Photograph any existing scratches or cracks, since those are the usual argument.
Photograph the screen with a plain white page open.
Note the accessories you are leaving: the charger, the bag, the memory card.
Back up the files, and sign out of accounts before handing it over.

body.text: You will see the serial number in the photograph, which is the number the receipt should repeat. A receipt without it can belong to any machine of the same model.

body.alt: A phone photographing a laptop serial number sticker.
body.caption: Serial number, photographed before the machine leaves your hands. The receipt should repeat it exactly.

body.text: It looks like a repair shop can be trusted because it is a shop. Most can, and the paperwork is what protects you from the few that cannot.
Three questions at the counter

items: What do you think the fault is, and what will the diagnosis cost?
Is the diagnosis charge separate from the repair?
What is the warranty on the repair, and how long is it?
Will you return the old part to me?
When should I expect it, and will you call if the price changes?
Can you write all of that on the receipt?

body.text: A shop that answers these easily is a shop worth using. A shop that answers vaguely is telling you something useful before any money is spent.

body.alt: A repair receipt showing a serial number, a fault description, and a price.
body.caption: A receipt with the serial number, the fault, the price, and the warranty period. Four lines that settle most arguments.

body.text: Ask for the old part
The part that comes out is proof that the part you paid for went in.

items: Ask before the work starts, not after.
Keep the old drive if it holds your files, and destroy it safely later.
Keep a replaced battery or fan for a month, in case the fault returns.
Ask them to write on the receipt that the part was returned.
Do not accept a part from another machine in place of yours.
Dispose of a dead battery at a shop that handles them, never in household waste.

body.text: None of this is distrust. It is the same habit as keeping a receipt for anything else, and the good shops expect it.
Do not worry about seeming difficult. A clear question at the counter is easier for the shop than an argument a week later.

body.alt: A replaced laptop fan and an old battery on a bench.
body.caption: The old part, handed back. It proves the repair happened, and it is your evidence if the fault returns.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here happens in real shops, and the paperwork is what helps.

items: The price rises after diagnosis: ask for a call before any work, as agreed in writing.
The fault returns within the warranty: take it back with the receipt, not with an explanation.
A new scratch appeared: show the photograph taken before the drop-off.
They cannot find the fault: take the machine elsewhere, and keep the diagnosis note.
They kept the old part: ask for it again, citing the receipt line.
They lost the machine: the serial number on the receipt is the record.

body.text: Practice
Prepare one device, even if nothing is wrong.

items: Photograph the serial number and the back of the device.
Write the fault in one sentence.
Write the three questions on a card.
Note the accessories you would leave.
Decide where the old part would be kept.

body.text: You can now leave a device for repair without losing control of it. In the next lesson you will make one machine last ten years.

excerpt: Keeping an older laptop useful: the drive and memory that matter, the battery habits that help, and the light system that gives it a second life.

body.text: This lesson is about making one laptop last ten years. You will choose the upgrades that matter, set the battery habits that help, and decide when a lighter system is the right second life for an old machine.
Laptops do not wear out evenly. The drive, the memory, and the battery fail first, and each is replaceable, which is why an old machine can stay useful long after its replacement date.
Before you start

items: The laptop, and its model number.
A notebook for costs.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: The three things worth doing

items: Replace a mechanical drive with a solid-state one, which is the largest single improvement.
Add memory up to eight gigabytes, if the machine allows it.
Clean the fan and vents once a year, which prevents the heat that kills boards.
Replace the battery when it no longer lasts an hour.
Keep the operating system updated, since older systems lose support.
Avoid installing every program offered, which is what fills a small drive.

body.text: You will see the machine start in seconds rather than minutes after the drive change, which feels like a new laptop. That single upgrade is usually worth more than everything else combined.

body.alt: An older laptop working on a bench with a document open.
body.caption: An older machine doing real work. Most of what limits it is the drive, the memory, and the dust.

body.text: It looks like an old laptop cannot run modern software. Much of what most people do is a browser and a document, and both run on modest hardware.
Battery habits that add years

items: Keep the charge between twenty and eighty per cent where the settings allow.
Use the charge limit feature if the maker provides one.
Avoid leaving it plugged in at a hundred per cent for days.
Do not work on a bed, where the vents are blocked.
Store it at half charge if you will not use it for a month.
Replace the battery rather than working with a swollen one.

body.text: The battery setting will show a limit option on many machines, such as stop charging at eighty per cent. That single switch is the difference between two years and four.

body.alt: A laptop settings screen showing a battery charge limit at eighty per cent.
body.caption: A charge limit of eighty per cent, set once. The battery spends its life away from the two states that age it fastest.

body.text: A lighter system for an old machine
When a machine struggles, a lighter operating system can give it another three years for the cost of an evening.

items: Choose a light Linux system designed for older hardware.
Try it from a memory stick first, without installing anything.
Check that the wifi, sound, and printer work before committing.
Keep the old system's files on an external drive.
Ask somebody who uses it, since the help is easier to find that way.
Install it only if you are comfortable trying a different desktop.

body.text: None of this needs a new machine. A drive, a stick of memory, and a clean fan are the whole list for most five-year-old laptops.
Do not worry about the machine being old. The work most people do has not become heavier, and the hardware has been good enough for years.

body.alt: A laptop showing a plain, light desktop environment.
body.caption: A plain desktop on old hardware. Fewer effects mean more of the machine is left for the work.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a decision about spending, and each has a sensible answer.

items: The machine is too slow after upgrades: check the drive health and the heat.
A new part does not fit: return it, and check the model number first.
The battery swells: stop using the machine, and replace it at a shop.
The light system will not install: return to the old system, which is why you tested from a stick.
The screen fails: a replacement screen costs less than a new laptop on most models.
The cost of repairs passes a third of a new machine: buy new, and keep the old drive.

body.text: Practice
Price three upgrades before deciding anything.

items: Look up your model's drive type and memory limit.
Price a solid-state drive and a memory stick.
Check whether a charge limit exists in the settings.
Note the cost of a battery replacement.
Compare the total with the price of a new machine.

body.text: You can now keep a machine useful long past its sale date. In the next lesson you will see how the internet reaches a house.
